Although
awl-THO
conj.
From all and though: grant that, admitting that. Webster 1828: grant all this; be it so; suppose that. Habakkuk uses it to build the greatest statement of faith without evidence in the Old Testament.

Biblical Definition

The last chapter of Habakkuk contains a sentence that has carried the church through every kind of loss, and its whole force rests on this conjunction: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls (Habakkuk 3:17). Six clauses of total agricultural ruin — and then verse 18: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The prophet does not deny the ruin, minimize it, or expect it to be reversed; he grants the whole of it and rejoices anyway, in God rather than in circumstances. Jeremiah uses the word to make the covenant breach more painful, not less: which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD (Jeremiah 31:32) — the sentence that introduces the promise of the new covenant. And Exodus uses it of a route not taken: God led Israel not by the way of the Philistines, although that was near (Exodus 13:17), because the short road went past war.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ALTHOUGH as grant all this; be it so; allow all; suppose that; admitting that — a conjunction that concedes a fact and then sets a stronger fact against it.

expand to see more

ALTHOUGH, conj. — Grant all this; be it so; allow all.

Suppose it to be so; admitting that; notwithstanding.

It concedes the truth of what follows it, and then subordinates it to the main clause.

Compare THOUGH, of the same force but weaker; NOTWITHSTANDING, of the same use.

From all and though; the all is intensive — grant it entirely.

Key Scripture

Habakkuk 3:17 — "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:"

Habakkuk 3:18 — "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation."

Jeremiah 31:32 — "Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD:"

Exodus 13:17 — "And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt:"

Modern Corruption

Habakkuk 3:17-18 rejoices while granting the whole disaster, which is neither the denial that positive-confession teaching requires nor the resignation that fatalism produces.

expand to see more

Habakkuk does not confess the fig tree into blossom. He states the ruin in six clauses, refuses none of them, and then rejoices in the LORD — the joy is located in God, not in a reversal of circumstances he expects. This is fatal to the positive-confession teaching that treats the naming of a hard fact as an act of unbelief which helps to produce it; Scripture’s prophets name hard facts constantly and are commended for it. It is equally distant from stoic resignation, which manages the loss by lowering the value of what was lost. Habakkuk does neither. He grants that the loss is total and real, and rejoices in a God who is neither the loss nor the compensation for it. The verse following supplies the ground: The LORD God is my strength.

Exodus 13:17 shows the conjunction doing quieter work, and it is one of the most pastorally useful verses in the Pentateuch. God did not lead Israel by the near way although that was near, because the short road ran past war they were not ready for. The nearest route is not always the appointed one, and the reason given is mercy toward a people God knew would turn back. This is the doctrine of providence at the level of a road: God’s ordering of means takes account of what His people can bear, which is exactly what 1 Corinthians 10:13 promises. Any account of guidance that assumes the shortest and most obvious path must be the right one has not read the verse.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ki (H3588), a versatile particle rendered although, for, when; im (H518), if, though; Greek kaiper (G2539), although, and yet.

expand to see more

Hebrew ki (H3588) — a particle of wide range, here concessive: although the fig tree shall not blossom (Habakkuk 3:17).

Hebrew asher (H834) — the relative, used concessively; although I was an husband unto them (Jeremiah 31:32).

Hebrew baal (H1166) — to be master or husband; the covenant relation Israel broke (Jeremiah 31:32).

Greek kaiper (G2539) — although, and yet; the New Testament concessive, used of Christ in Hebrews 5:8.

Hebrew alaz (H5937) — to exult, to rejoice; Habakkuk’s answering verb in 3:18.

Usage

"Although the fig tree shall not blossom... yet I will rejoice in the LORD (Habakkuk 3:17-18) — the ruin granted in full, and joy located in God."

"Which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them (Jeremiah 31:32) — the concession that makes the breach worse."

"God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near (Exodus 13:17) — the nearest road is not always the appointed one."
